lesson.title: Stuck on What It's For: How Functional Fixedness Blocks Creative Solutions
lesson.summary: Functional fixedness is the tendency to see an object only in terms of its typical use, which blocks people from noticing its other possible functions when solving a problem.
lesson.body:
Functional fixedness is the tendency to think of an object only in terms of the function it is normally used for, which makes it hard to notice that the same object could serve a completely different purpose. It is a specific case of the broader phenomenon of mental set, the general tendency to keep applying a problem-solving approach that has worked in the past even when the current problem calls for something different. Where mental set is about getting stuck on a strategy, functional fixedness is about getting stuck on an object's conventional identity, treating a screwdriver as only a tool for turning screws rather than, say, a lever or a paint stirrer.

The reason this happens is rooted in ordinary learning. Every time a person uses an object for its typical purpose, the association between that object and that purpose gets strengthened and becomes more automatic to retrieve. This is efficient most of the time, since it lets people reach for familiar tools without reinventing their purpose from scratch. But when a novel problem needs an unconventional use for that same object, the well-practiced, typical function comes to mind first and crowds out less familiar possibilities, much the way a strong prototype can crowd out atypical category members in ordinary categorization.

The classic demonstration of functional fixedness is Karl Duncker's candle problem. Participants are given a candle, a box of thumbtacks, and a book of matches, and are asked to attach the lit candle to a wall so that it does not drip wax on the table below. The solution is to empty the tacks out of their box, tack the empty box to the wall, and use it as a small platform for the candle. Many participants struggle with this because they perceive the box only as a container for holding the tacks, not as a potential tool in its own right. When the same tacks are instead presented already dumped out beside an empty box, participants solve the problem far more easily, because the box is no longer mentally fixed to the function of "container."

Functional fixedness connects closely to the same executive and conceptual flexibility involved in creativity and divergent thinking. Escaping functional fixedness requires generating multiple, less typical uses for a familiar object rather than settling immediately on its most conventional purpose, which is exactly what divergent thinking tasks like listing alternative uses for a brick or a paperclip are designed to train. It also requires inhibitory control to suppress the automatic, dominant response long enough for an unusual possibility to surface. In this sense, functional fixedness is what divergent thinking has to overcome, and practicing divergent thinking is one practical way people become better at breaking out of it.

Functional fixedness tends to grow stronger with more experience using an object in one particular way, since repeated use deepens the association between object and function. It also shows up beyond laboratory puzzles, in engineering design, improvisation, and everyday troubleshooting, where the person who solves a problem is often the one willing to see a familiar object, a paperclip, a phone book, a bottle cap, as something other than what it was built for. Design and brainstorming techniques often warm people up with alternative-use exercises specifically because doing so temporarily loosens the grip of an object's usual function before real problem solving begins.
